title: Galaxy cluster MACS0416 (Hubble and Webb composite image)
caption: The galaxy cluster MACS0416, imaged by the James Webb and Hubble Space Telescopes
celestial: MACS J0416.1-2403 · constellation Eridanus · about 4 billion light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, J. Diego (Instituto de Física de Cantabria, Spain), J. D’Silva (U. Western Australia), A. Koekemoer (STScI), J. Summers & R. Windhorst (ASU), and H. Yan (U. Missouri)

recognition.text: Ranked #90 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Dozens of yellowish spiral and elliptical galaxies gather in the middle of this picture, surrounded by distorted streaks that seem to follow invisible circles around the center, while red and blue galaxies crowd the rest of the field. This is the galaxy cluster MACS0416, about 4.3 billion light-years away, in a view combining Webb infrared data with Hubble visible light.

The light we see from the cluster left it shortly after our Solar System formed. Its gravity magnifies galaxies far behind it through gravitational lensing, creating those streaks, and the team has used it to spot supernovae and even single stars magnified enormously.

Color here hints at distance. The bluest galaxies are relatively nearby and often forming stars intensely, which Hubble detects best. The redder ones tend to be farther away or very dusty, which Webb detects best. Together the two telescopes cover wavelengths from 0.4 to 5 microns.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.22 x 2.06 arcminutes) and distance (4 billion light years), the frame spans roughly 2.6 million × 2.4 million light-years. Its light set out about 4,000 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS and WFC3 and Webb's NIRCam were combined. Blue shows Hubble's shortest wavelengths, green intermediate Hubble and Webb data, and red Webb's longest infrared wavelengths.
understand.eye: Much of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye. Only Hubble's shortest wavelengths fall in the range we can see.

explore: In general, the shortest wavelengths were colored blue, the longest red, and those in between green. The result has been described as among the most colorful pictures of the universe yet made, and it holds details that could only be captured by combining both space telescopes.
alt: A cluster of dozens of yellowish galaxies at the center, surrounded by curved, stretched streaks and many red and blue galaxies of various shapes on a black background.
